prompt: Against which of these does encrypting the planner's data at rest help?

choices.text: A debugger on a rooted phone while the app runs
choices.why: The keys are in memory then.

choices.text: Malware running as the app and asking for the sessions the way the app's own code does
choices.why: It gets the data decrypted, as the app would.

choices.text: A thief with the locked phone
choices.why: Right. The storage is unreadable without the key the lock protects.

choices.text: The owner, signed in
choices.why: It is her data, and she should read it.

prompt: The lesson says three rows of its table are not failures of encryption. What defends against code that runs as the app?

choices.text: Few, reviewed dependencies, no code from a server, and less data kept
choices.why: Right. That is a different job from encryption.

choices.text: A second layer of encryption with a stronger key
choices.why: That code would be handed the second key too.

choices.text: Turning on biometric unlock
choices.why: Once unlocked, the app's code runs with the data available.

choices.text: The iOS class `complete`
choices.why: It protects a locked phone, not a running app.

prompt: What is the default Data Protection class for an iOS app's files?

choices.text: complete
choices.why: That is the strictest, and an app must ask for it.

choices.text: none
choices.why: That is the weakest, and not the default.

choices.text: completeUnlessOpen
choices.why: That keeps an open file writable after the lock.

choices.text: completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication
choices.why: Right. Readable from the first unlock until the phone is turned off.

prompt: Match each kind of storage to when it can be read.

pairs.right: only while the phone is unlocked
after the first unlock since boot
as soon as the phone boots

prompt: Why does the lesson store the planner's key with `ThisDeviceOnly`?

choices.text: It makes the Keychain faster
choices.why: Speed is not affected.

choices.text: So a backup restored elsewhere arrives without its key
choices.why: Right. The key stays on the phone that made it.

choices.text: Apple requires it for every app in the store
choices.why: It is a choice, and the lesson argues for it.

choices.text: Without it, the item is deleted when the phone locks
choices.why: Locking does not delete Keychain items.

prompt: In envelope encryption, what encrypts the planner's sessions?

choices.text: The key-encryption key, used directly
choices.why: That one wraps the data key; it never touches the data.

choices.text: The data key
choices.why: Right. It is stored on the disk only in wrapped form.

choices.text: The person's passcode
choices.why: The passcode protects the platform's keys, not this one directly.

choices.text: The nonce
choices.why: A nonce is not a key; it makes each seal different.

prompt: Two seals of the same six sessions gave different bytes. Why does the lesson want that?

choices.text: Different bytes compress better on the phone's storage
choices.why: Ciphertext does not compress either way.

choices.text: The data key changes on each seal
choices.why: The key stayed the same; the nonce changed.

choices.text: So the server can tell the two versions apart
choices.why: The server never sees this file.

choices.text: Reusing a nonce with one key leaks data and lets tags be forged
choices.why: Right. A fresh random nonce per seal is the rule GCM needs.

prompt: One bit of sessions.enc was flipped. What did `node crypt.ts open` do?

choices.text: Refused the whole file
choices.why: Right: Unsupported state or unable to authenticate data.

choices.text: Opened all six, one of them with a wrong date
choices.why: That is exactly what the tag prevents.

choices.text: Opened five sessions and skipped the damaged one
choices.why: GCM decrypts all of it or none.

choices.text: Asked for the key-encryption key again
choices.why: The key was there; the data had changed.

prompt: How many bytes long is the nonce crypt.ts writes at the start of the sealed file?
A whole SQLite database encrypted page by page with AES-256 is what ___ provides.
What makes a biometric check worth something, according to the lesson?

choices.text: It returns success: true to the app
choices.why: That boolean is what malware or a debugger flips.

choices.text: It runs before the app's first screen is drawn
choices.why: When it runs changes nothing if the key was available anyway.

choices.text: Passing it is what releases the key
choices.why: Right. No check, no key, no data.

choices.text: It uses the face rather than a finger
choices.why: Face or finger, the question is what passing it unlocks.

prompt: A person adds a new fingerprint to their phone. The planner's key was created with `biometryCurrentSet`. What happens next time it opens?

choices.text: The key no longer works: sign in again, then resync
choices.why: Right. Somebody who learnt the passcode cannot add their own finger to reach the data.

choices.text: The planner asks the Keychain to copy the key to the new finger
choices.why: Keys are not copied; this one is invalidated.

choices.text: The new finger unlocks it, since the phone trusts it
choices.why: That is what the flag exists to stop.

choices.text: Nothing changes
choices.why: The flag ties the key to the fingers enrolled when it was made.

prompt: In Expo, when is `authenticateAsync()` from expo-local-authentication the right tool?

choices.text: As the lock on the planner's encrypted database
choices.why: It returns a boolean, which is the curtain the section warns about.

choices.text: To generate the data key
choices.why: It generates nothing.

choices.text: As a confirmation before something the server checks again
choices.why: Right. The server's check is the real one there.

choices.text: To replace expo-secure-store
choices.why: SecureStore with requireAuthentication is what ties the key to the check.

prompt: Put in order what happens when the planner opens its sealed sessions behind a biometric.
items: the system shows the biometric prompt
the hardware unwraps the data key
the data key opens sessions.enc, checking its tag
the data key is let go

prompt: A planner keeps its data key in a file beside the encrypted database, unwrapped. Which row of the threat table does it lose?

choices.text: The owner, who can no longer read her own sessions
choices.why: She reads them fine; that is not the loss.

choices.text: The backup
choices.why: Right. A copy of the sandbox carries the lock and the key taped to it.

choices.text: Malware running as the app
choices.why: That row was lost to encryption of any kind.

choices.text: None: a key on the disk is as safe as one in the Keystore
choices.why: The Keystore's keys cannot be copied out; a file can.

prompt: After the key-encryption key is gone, which does the lesson say the planner should do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: treat the sealed file as no data
choices.why: It cannot be opened, and pretending otherwise helps nobody.

choices.text: bring the sessions back with a full resync
choices.why: Lesson 12's resync does exactly that.

choices.text: try every nonce until the file opens
choices.why: The nonce is in the file; the key is what is missing.

choices.text: turn the encryption off for next time
choices.why: That throws away the protection to avoid a resync.

prompt: A planner for therapy sessions syncs only while open. Which iOS class does the lesson's reasoning point to for its database?

choices.text: none, so the sync never fails
choices.why: That leaves health data readable on a locked phone.

choices.text: the default, as for every app
choices.why: The default suits apps that sync in the background with the screen off.

choices.text: completeUnlessOpen, to keep the file open
choices.why: That is for a download finishing after the lock.

choices.text: complete
choices.why: Right. It needs no reads while locked, so it can have the strictest class.

prompt: Why does the lesson insist on another way in besides the biometric?

choices.text: The Keystore expires biometric keys every month
choices.why: It does not; enrolment changes invalidate them.

choices.text: Biometrics are illegal in some countries
choices.why: Not the lesson's argument.

choices.text: A face goes unrecognised in the dark, or a person has no biometric
choices.why: Right. A biometric is a convenience over a secret.

choices.text: The store rejects apps that use biometrics alone without a password screen
choices.why: The argument is the person in the dark, not a store rule.
